SUPREME: A Multi-GPU Framework for Reproducible Image Unlearning Method Evaluation

Petros Andreou Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, School of Science, Loughborough University, Loughborough, UK E-mail {p.andreou2, j.lanyon, g.cosma}@lboro.ac.uk    Jamie Lanyon Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, School of Science, Loughborough University, Loughborough, UK E-mail {p.andreou2, j.lanyon, g.cosma}@lboro.ac.uk    Axel Finke Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, School of Science, Loughborough University, Loughborough, UK E-mail {p.andreou2, j.lanyon, g.cosma}@lboro.ac.uk Affiliation: School of Mathematics, Statistics and Physics, Newcastle University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 7RU, UK E-mail axel.finke@newcastle.ac.uk    Georgina Cosma Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, School of Science, Loughborough University, Loughborough, UK E-mail {p.andreou2, j.lanyon, g.cosma}@lboro.ac.uk
Abstract

Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training data from a trained model without retraining it from scratch. Evaluating an unlearning method requires repeating training, unlearning, and evaluation across multiple seeds, which is computationally expensive. To our knowledge, existing image classification unlearning frameworks run on a single GPU, which limits how many seeds can be evaluated in reasonable time. We introduce SUPREME, an open-source framework that distributes these stages across multiple GPUs. SUPREME makes three contributions: a registry-based design for adding new methods, metrics, models, and scenarios; a multi-GPU architecture supporting multiple accelerators and precision modes; and a demonstration on Pins Face Recognition using ResNet18 and ViT under full-class and random-sample unlearning across ten seeds. The framework is available at https://github.com/pedroandreou/supreme-unlearning.

Keywords: 
Machine unlearning Distributed framework Evaluation

1 Introduction

Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training data from a trained model without retraining it from scratch. Several approximate methods have been proposed, including fine-tuning, teacher–student distillation [3], impair-and-repair schemes [13], and parameter-importance methods [7, 8]. Evaluating these methods requires metrics spanning multiple criteria: forgetting (how much forget-set knowledge is removed), utility (how well retain-set performance is preserved), behavioural and parametric equivalence to a model retrained on the retain set, and privacy (for example, resistance to membership inference attacks).

Three factors motivate reproducible evaluation of unlearning. First, the number of proposed methods and metrics is increasing, and comparing them under the same training setup and seeds is required to identify which methods perform best. Second, evaluation now covers larger model architectures such as Vision Transformers and larger datasets, which increases the compute cost of every training run. Third, recent work shows that single-seed results can misrepresent a method’s performance, because outcomes depend on initial weights, data ordering, and the stochasticity of the unlearning step [2, 11]. Repeating the full pipeline across multiple seeds is therefore required for a consistent comparison.

Evaluation frameworks for image classification unlearning include MUBox [12], which benchmarks methods across several scenarios; ERASURE [4], a modular toolkit for different data domains; and Deep Unlearn [2], which tests methods across multiple random initialisations. Each runs on a single GPU at full precision, and of these only Deep Unlearn supports multi-seed evaluation.

We introduce SUPREME (Standardised Unlearning Platform for Reproducible Method Evaluation), an open-source framework for image classification unlearning. Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    An extensible framework with a registry-based design covering datasets, model architectures, unlearning methods, evaluation metrics, and unlearning scenarios. New components are added by implementing an interface and registering a module path, without modifying framework code.

  • •

    A hardware-agnostic architecture with multi-GPU support built on PyTorch and Lightning Fabric, including DDP, FSDP, and DeepSpeed ZeRO. Distribution applies to training, unlearning, and evaluation — to our knowledge the first image classification unlearning framework to do so.

  • •

    A demonstration on Pins Face Recognition. We evaluate the integrated methods on ResNet18 and ViT under full-class and random-sample unlearning across ten seeds.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 presents the SUPREME framework, Section 3 details the experimental methodology, and Section 4 reports and discusses the results. The appendices provide the component registry (Appendix 0.A), the metric definitions (Appendix 0.B), and additional results (Appendix 0.C).

2 SUPREME Framework

2.1 Notation

Let MinitM_{\mathrm{init}} be a model parameterised by initial weights which may be randomly initialised or pre-trained and let MoM_{\mathrm{o}} be the model trained on some training set DD consisting of image–label pairs (x,y)(x,y). Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of some forget set Df⊆DD_{\mathrm{f}}\subseteq D from MoM_{\mathrm{o}}. This is done by applying some unlearning method to MoM_{\mathrm{o}} to obtain an unlearned model MuM_{\mathrm{u}}. The goal is that MuM_{\mathrm{u}} mimics as closely as possible the retrained baseline MrM_{\mathrm{r}}, i.e., the model which has been trained from scratch on the retain set Dr≔D∖DfD_{\mathrm{r}}\coloneqq D\setminus D_{\mathrm{f}}. Unlearning performance is assessed by evaluating MuM_{\mathrm{u}} on a test forget set Df′D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime} and a test retain set Dr′D_{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime} which we now specify based on some unseen dataset D′D^{\prime}.

SUPREME supports two types of unlearning scenarios: targeted and random-sample unlearning. These differ in how the set of forget targets CC is defined:

  • •

    Targeted unlearning removes a label-defined subset of the training data, i.e., each c∈Cc\in C is a class (or sub-class) label and the corresponding forget set is Df≔{(x,y)∈D∣y=c}D_{\mathrm{f}}\coloneqq\{(x,y)\in D\mid y=c\}.

  • •

    Random-sample unlearning removes a random subset of the training samples, i.e., each c∈Cc\in C is a number in (0,1](0,1] and the corresponding forget set DfD_{\mathrm{f}} is a subset – sampled uniformly at random – of DD of size ⌈c​|D|⌉\lceil c|D|\rceil.

The two scenarios also differ in how the forget and retain test sets, Df′D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime} and Dr′D_{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime}, are defined: targeted unlearning uses held-out samples of the forgotten target (Df′≔{(x,y)∈D′∣y=c}D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime}\coloneqq\{(x,y)\in D^{\prime}\mid y=c\} and Dr′≔D′∖Df′D_{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime}\coloneqq D^{\prime}\setminus D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime}) to test whether unlearning generalises beyond the training samples, while random-sample unlearning has no such held-out set and evaluates on the training forget samples directly (Df′≔DfD_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime}\coloneqq D_{\mathrm{f}} and Dr′≔D′D_{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime}\coloneqq D^{\prime}).

2.2 Pipeline

Figure 1 shows the SUPREME pipeline and Algorithm 1 provides details. Stage 1 trains MoM_{\mathrm{o}} on DD. For each forget target c∈Cc\in C, the framework trains MrM_{\mathrm{r}} on DrD_{\mathrm{r}}. For each unlearning method a∈Aa\in A, Stage 2 applies aa to MoM_{\mathrm{o}} to obtain MuM_{\mathrm{u}}, and Stage 3 evaluates MuM_{\mathrm{u}} against MrM_{\mathrm{r}} using the configured metrics. The pipeline has three properties: seeded randomness, distributed execution, and registry-based extensibility.

Seeded randomness. Each seed determines initial weights, data ordering, the random forget-set draw (under the random-sample scenario), and the stochastic operations inside the unlearning step. Running every method under the same seed configuration ensures that every a∈Aa\in A is evaluated under identical starting conditions for a given seed, isolating method differences from pipeline randomness. The framework allows independent seeds for the training, unlearning, and evaluation stages, enabling users to isolate the effect of each stage when needed.

Distributed execution. All three stages execute across PP devices. Training and unlearning use gradient synchronisation, where gradients are averaged across devices after each backward pass so all devices apply the same parameter update. Evaluation uses result aggregation, where per-batch metric values are collected across devices and averaged into the final metric value. Distribution applies to every stage, including the retrained baseline, which dominates total runtime when |C||C| or the number of seeds is large.

Registry-based extensibility. Datasets, model architectures, unlearning methods, evaluation metrics, and unlearning scenarios are registered via module paths. New components are added by implementing the required interface and registering the module path, without modifying framework code.

2.3 Implementation

SUPREME is built on PyTorch and Lightning Fabric. The framework supports DDP, FSDP, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-1/2/3 as distributed strategies, selectable at runtime. Two optimisations reduce per-run overhead when the pipeline is repeated across many seeds: enabling tensor cores for matrix operations, and accelerated model initialisation that defers parameter materialisation until the model is moved to its device.

Vision models. SUPREME registers two model architectures. ResNet18 [10] is a four-block residual convolutional network with 64–512 channels per block, trained from scratch on 32×3232\times 32 inputs. ViT [6] is fine-tuned from google/vit-base-patch16-224, which divides 224×224224\times 224 inputs into 16×1616\times 16 patches and processes them through 12 transformer layers with 12 attention heads and 768 hidden dimensions. Depending on the selected distributed strategy, the weights, optimiser state, and gradients of these models (shown in Stages 1–2 of Figure 1) are replicated across the PP devices (DDP) or partitioned among them (FSDP and DeepSpeed ZeRO).

Image preprocessing. ResNet18 inputs are resized to 32×3232\times 32 with standard training-time augmentation (random crop, horizontal flip, rotation) and per-channel normalisation computed from the training set. ViT inputs are resized to 256×256256\times 256, centre-cropped to 224×224224\times 224, horizontally flipped, and normalised with ImageNet statistics, as required by the pre-trained model. Augmentation is disabled during unlearning and evaluation.

Hardware support. SUPREME’s architecture supports multi-GPU execution. Because distributed gradient averaging introduces non-determinism, multi-GPU runs do not exactly reproduce single-device results; the experiments in this paper therefore use a single device (Section 3).

Evaluation metrics. Unlearning quality is evaluated under seven criteria: behavioural equivalence, parametric equivalence, privacy, forgetting, utility, efficiency, and resources. Definitions and the metrics under each criterion are in Table 3 in Appendix 0.B.

3 Experimental Methodology

We demonstrate SUPREME on Pins Face Recognition [1], an image classification benchmark of 17,534 facial images across 105 celebrity identities. The preprocessing follows Section 2.3. ResNet18 uses statistics computed from the training set, μ=(0.516,0.419,0.373)\mu=(0.516,0.419,0.373) and σ=(0.286,0.255,0.246)\sigma=(0.286,0.255,0.246). ViT uses ImageNet statistics, μ=(0.485,0.456,0.406)\mu=(0.485,0.456,0.406) and σ=(0.229,0.224,0.225)\sigma=(0.229,0.224,0.225). We evaluate two unlearning scenarios. Full-class unlearning removes all samples for five identities: alex_lawther, bill_gates, danielle_panabaker, hugh_jackman, and josh_radnor. Random-sample unlearning removes a 0.1 % subset of training samples drawn from across all classes. We use I=10I=10 training runs with seeds 260–269 (the training-seed index ii in Algorithm 1 maps to these values), with a single unlearning and evaluation seed per training seed (J=K=1J=K=1). Varying the training seed surfaces the across-seed variance reported in Section 4; the separate training, unlearning, and evaluation seeds (sts_{\mathrm{t}}, sus_{\mathrm{u}}, ses_{\mathrm{e}}) that Algorithm 1 also supports would decompose that variance further but are not needed for this demonstration. At J=K=1J=K=1, the seed formulae in Algorithm 1 reduce to su=se=sts_{\mathrm{u}}=s_{\mathrm{e}}=s_{\mathrm{t}}. The unlearning methods listed in Table 2 in Appendix 0.A are applied to MoM_{\mathrm{o}}, with MrM_{\mathrm{r}} as the baseline. The experiments were run on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU (48 GB VRAM) to maintain exact numerical parity with the reference implementations [3, 7, 8], following the same choice made by OpenUnlearning [5] in the text domain.

4 Results and Discussion

Table 1 reports the test-accuracy differences between MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} on Df′D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime} (Δ​AccDf′\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime}}) and Dr′D_{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime} (Δ​AccDr′\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{D_{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime}}), and the layer-wise weight distance Layer\mathrm{Layer} between the two models. Table 4 in Appendix 0.C reports activation distances and membership inference attack (MIA) score differences (Δ​MIA\Delta\mathrm{MIA}). Together these cover four of the seven evaluation criteria in Table 3 in Appendix 0.B: forgetting, utility, parametric equivalence, and privacy.

Across-seed variance. Several method-and-scenario combinations produced large standard deviations over the ten seeds. The two largest forget-set accuracy (Δ​AccDf′\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime}}) standard deviations both occurred in the random-sample scenario. Random Labels on ResNet18 gave Δ​AccDf′=−48.89±34.03\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime}}=-48.89\pm 34.03 percentage points, and Selective Synaptic Dampening on ViT gave −55.00±37.99-55.00\pm 37.99. A single seed can therefore differ from the ten-seed mean by tens of percentage points. Because only the training seed is varied (J=K=1J=K=1; see Section 3), the observed spread combines four sources of randomness: initial weights, data ordering, the random forget-set draw, and stochastic operations inside the unlearning method.

Multi-criterion reporting. In the full-class scenario, the mean MIA difference (Δ​MIA\Delta\mathrm{MIA}) in Table 4 stays within ±0.05\pm 0.05 for every method on both model architectures, and seven of the twelve satisfy |Δ​MIA|≤0.02|\Delta\mathrm{MIA}|\leq 0.02. On the same runs, Δ​AccDf′\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime}} ranges from 0.000.00 to 89.4489.44 percentage points on ResNet18 and from 0.000.00 to 35.5235.52 on ViT. Δ​MIA\Delta\mathrm{MIA} therefore does not separate the methods in this setting, whereas Δ​AccDf′\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{D_{\mathrm{f}}^{\prime}} does. The methods may have similar privacy behaviour, or the MIA probe may be too weak on Pins Face Recognition.

5 Conclusion

We introduced SUPREME, an open-source framework for evaluating image classification unlearning, registry-based across datasets, model architectures, unlearning methods, evaluation metrics, and scenarios, and able to distribute training, unlearning, and evaluation across multiple devices through Lightning Fabric. Our single-GPU demonstration on Pins Face Recognition produced ten-seed results across both model architectures and both scenarios. The demonstration is confined to a single dataset, two architectures, and a single device, so the reported numbers characterise the framework rather than a definitive ranking of the methods; broader conclusions would require the larger-scale, multi-seed studies the framework is designed to enable. Future work will extend the demonstration to the other registered components and use the per-stage seeds to decompose the across-seed spread into its training, unlearning, and evaluation parts.

Appendix 0.A SUPREME Component Registry

Appendix 0.B Unlearning Metrics

The following metrics evaluate machine unlearning quality by comparing the unlearned model MuM_{\mathrm{u}} against the retrained model MrM_{\mathrm{r}}. In the following definitions, MM denotes some model (e.g., the unlearned or retrained model). Throughout, M⁡(x)∈ΔK−1M(x)\in\Delta^{K-1} denotes the softmax probability vector produced by MM on input xx, where KK is the number of classes and ΔK−1\Delta^{K-1} is the (K−1)(K-1)-simplex. D~\tilde{D} denotes some generic dataset.

0.B.1 Model evaluation metrics

Layer-wise distance. Layer-wise distance quantifies parameter changes during unlearning by measuring the Euclidean distance between the weights of MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}}:

Layer≔∑l=1L∑i=1nl(wul,i−wrl,i)2∈[0,+∞),\mathrm{Layer}\coloneqq\sqrt{\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{l}}(w_{\mathrm{u}}^{l,i}-w_{\mathrm{r}}^{l,i})^{2}}\in[0,+\infty), (1)

where wul,iw_{\mathrm{u}}^{l,i} and wrl,iw_{\mathrm{r}}^{l,i} represent the iith weight parameter in layer ll of models MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} respectively, nln_{l} denotes the number of learnable parameters in layer ll, and LL is the total number of layers. Smaller distance indicates better unlearning (zero means MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} have identical weights); larger distance indicates worse unlearning.

Activation distance. Activation distance quantifies the difference between the final-layer activations of MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} on D~\tilde{D}. Implementations include the L1-norm between softmax outputs [9] and the L2-norm [3]; this work uses L2-norm:

ActivD~≔1|D~|​∑(x,y)∈D~‖Mr​(x)−Mu​(x)‖22∈[0,2],\mathrm{Activ}_{\tilde{D}}\coloneqq\sqrt{\frac{1}{|\tilde{D}|}\sum_{(x,y)\in\tilde{D}}\|M_{\mathrm{r}}(x)-M_{\mathrm{u}}(x)\|_{2}^{2}}\in[0,\sqrt{2}], (2)

where ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} is the Euclidean norm. Smaller activation distance indicates better unlearning (zero means MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} produce identical outputs on samples in D~\tilde{D}); larger distance indicates worse unlearning.

JS-Divergence. Jensen–Shannon divergence symmetrically quantifies similarity between probability distributions, derived from the Kullback–Leibler divergence. It compares output distributions of MrM_{\mathrm{r}} and MuM_{\mathrm{u}} on D~\tilde{D}:

JSD~≔12​|D~|∑(x′,y′)∈D~[KL(Mr(x′)∥m(x′))+KL(Mu(x′)∥m(x′))]∈[0,1],\displaystyle\mathrm{JS}_{\tilde{D}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2|\tilde{D}|}\sum_{(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in\tilde{D}}\Bigl[\mathrm{KL}(M_{\mathrm{r}}(x^{\prime})\parallel m(x^{\prime}))+\mathrm{KL}(M_{\mathrm{u}}(x^{\prime})\parallel m(x^{\prime}))\Bigr]\in[0,1], (3)

where m⁡(x′)≔(Mr​(x′)+Mu​(x′))/2m(x^{\prime})\coloneqq(M_{\mathrm{r}}(x^{\prime})+M_{\mathrm{u}}(x^{\prime}))/2 is the average output of both models for sample x′x^{\prime} in D~\tilde{D}, and KL(⋅∥⋅)\mathrm{KL}(\,\cdot\,\!\parallel\!\,\cdot\,) is the Kullback–Leibler divergence. Lower JS-divergence indicates better unlearning (zero means MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} produce identical output distributions on samples in D~\tilde{D}; one means completely different distributions).

Completeness. Completeness quantifies prediction consistency between MrM_{\mathrm{r}} and MuM_{\mathrm{u}} on D~\tilde{D}. Predictions are considered complete when both models agree, regardless of correctness, focusing on consistency rather than accuracy:

ComplD~≔1|D~|∑(x,y)∈D~𝟏{argmaxk[Mr(x)]k=argmaxk[Mu(x)]k}∈[0,1],\displaystyle\mathrm{Compl}_{\tilde{D}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{|\tilde{D}|}\sum_{(x,y)\in\tilde{D}}\mathbf{1}\Bigl\{\argmax_{k}[M_{\mathrm{r}}(x)]_{k}=\argmax_{k}[M_{\mathrm{u}}(x)]_{k}\Bigr\}\in[0,1], (4)

where [z]k[z]_{k} is the kkth element of a vector zz, and argmaxk\argmax_{k} returns the class with the highest predicted probability. Lower completeness indicates worse unlearning (approaching zero means MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} produce completely different predictions on samples in D~\tilde{D}; one means identical predictions on all samples).

Accuracy. Accuracy differences (Δ​AccD~\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{\tilde{D}}) computes the difference in predictive performance between MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} on D~\tilde{D} [9]:

Δ​AccD~≔AccD~​(Mu)−AccD~​(Mr)∈[−1,1],\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{\tilde{D}}\coloneqq\mathrm{Acc}_{\tilde{D}}(M_{\mathrm{u}})-\mathrm{Acc}_{\tilde{D}}(M_{\mathrm{r}})\in[-1,1], (5)

where

AccD~(M)=1|D~|∑(x,y)∈D~𝟏{argmaxk[M(x)]k=y}∈[0,1].\mathrm{Acc}_{\tilde{D}}(M)=\frac{1}{|\tilde{D}|}\sum_{(x,y)\in\tilde{D}}\mathbf{1}\{\argmax_{k}[M(x)]_{k}=y\}\in[0,1]. (6)

When M=MuM=M_{\mathrm{u}} is the unlearned model, we suppress the argument and write AccD~≔AccD~​(Mu)\mathrm{Acc}_{\tilde{D}}\coloneqq\mathrm{Acc}_{\tilde{D}}(M_{\mathrm{u}}). Δ​AccD~\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{\tilde{D}} closer to zero indicates better unlearning (zero means MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} have identical accuracy on D~\tilde{D}); larger |Δ​AccD~||\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{\tilde{D}}| indicates worse unlearning.

Loss. Loss differences (Δ​LossD~\Delta\mathrm{Loss}_{\tilde{D}}) computes the difference in cross-entropy error between MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} on D~\tilde{D}:

Δ​LossD~=LossD~​(Mu)−LossD~​(Mr)∈ℝ,\Delta\mathrm{Loss}_{\tilde{D}}=\mathrm{Loss}_{\tilde{D}}(M_{\mathrm{u}})-\mathrm{Loss}_{\tilde{D}}(M_{\mathrm{r}})\in\mathbb{R}, (7)

where

LossD~(M)=−1|D~|∑(x,y)∈D~log[M(x)]y∈[0,+∞).\mathrm{Loss}_{\tilde{D}}(M)=-\frac{1}{|\tilde{D}|}\sum_{(x,y)\in\tilde{D}}\log[M(x)]_{y}\in[0,+\infty). (8)

When M=MuM=M_{\mathrm{u}} is the unlearned model, we suppress the argument and write LossD~≔LossD~​(Mu)\mathrm{Loss}_{\tilde{D}}\coloneqq\mathrm{Loss}_{\tilde{D}}(M_{\mathrm{u}}). Δ​LossD~\Delta\mathrm{Loss}_{\tilde{D}} closer to zero indicates better unlearning (zero means MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} have identical loss on D~\tilde{D}); larger |Δ​LossD~||\Delta\mathrm{Loss}_{\tilde{D}}| indicates worse unlearning.

Membership Inference Attack. Membership inference attack differences (Δ​MIA\Delta\mathrm{MIA}) measures the difference in data leakage risk between MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} on the forget training set, determining whether a data point was in the model’s training set DD. A logistic regression classifier trained on the entropy of softmax probabilities distinguishes DrD_{\mathrm{r}} (labelled as 1) from D′D^{\prime} (labelled as 0), then evaluates DfD_{\mathrm{f}} to measure retained information [3]:

Δ​MIA≔MIA⁡(Mu)−MIA⁡(Mr)∈[−1,1],\displaystyle\Delta\mathrm{MIA}\coloneqq\mathrm{MIA}(M_{\mathrm{u}})-\mathrm{MIA}(M_{\mathrm{r}})\in[-1,1], (9)

where

MIA(M)=1|Df|∑(x,y)∈Df𝟏{hϕ(e(M(x)))=1}∈[0,1].\mathrm{MIA}(M)=\frac{1}{|D_{\mathrm{f}}|}\sum_{(x,y)\in D_{\mathrm{f}}}\mathbf{1}\{h_{\phi}(e(M(x)))=1\}\in[0,1]. (10)

When M=MuM=M_{\mathrm{u}} is the unlearned model, we suppress the argument and write MIA≔MIA⁡(Mu)\mathrm{MIA}\coloneqq\mathrm{MIA}(M_{\mathrm{u}}). Above, 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the indicator function, hϕh_{\phi} is the logistic regression classifier with parameters ϕ\phi, trained on {(e⁡(M⁡(x)),1):(x,y)∈Dr}\{(e(M(x)),1):(x,y)\in D_{\mathrm{r}}\} (retain samples labelled as 1) and {(e⁡(M⁡(x)),0):(x,y)∈D′}\{(e(M(x)),0):(x,y)\in D^{\prime}\} (test samples labelled as 0), and e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) is the entropy function applied to the model output probabilities:

e(p)=−∑k=1Kpklogpk∈[0,logK],e(p)=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}\log p_{k}\in[0,\log K], (11)

where p=(p1,…,pK)∈ΔK−1p=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{K})\in\Delta^{K-1}. Values of Δ​MIA\Delta\mathrm{MIA} closer to zero indicates better unlearning (zero means MuM_{\mathrm{u}} and MrM_{\mathrm{r}} have identical membership inference vulnerability); larger |Δ​MIA||\Delta\mathrm{MIA}| indicates worse unlearning.

0.B.2 Computational Cost Metrics

The following metrics measure the computational cost of the unlearning procedure rather than the quality of the resulting model. They capture the practical viability and scalability of unlearning methods, measuring time and resource consumption during the execution of the unlearning method.

Time. Time measures the elapsed wall-clock duration of the unlearning procedure:

Time≔tend−tstart∈[0,+∞),\mathrm{Time}\coloneqq t_{\mathrm{end}}-t_{\mathrm{start}}\in[0,+\infty), (12)

where tstartt_{\mathrm{start}} is the timestamp recorded immediately before the unlearning method begins and tendt_{\mathrm{end}} is the timestamp recorded immediately after it terminates, both in seconds. Lower time indicates better efficiency; higher time indicates worse efficiency.

Memory Usage. Memory usage captures the peak memory consumed by the process during unlearning on the active accelerator (see Table 2) [14]:

Memory≔maxt∈[0,T]mt−mbaseline10243∈[0,+∞),\mathrm{Memory}\coloneqq\max_{t\in[0,T]}\frac{m_{t}-m_{\mathrm{baseline}}}{1024^{3}}\in[0,+\infty), (13)

where T≔TimeT\coloneqq\mathrm{Time} is the elapsed time defined in Eq. 12, t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] is a time point during the procedure, mtm_{t} is the amount of accelerator memory in bytes in use by the process at time tt (storing, e.g., model weights, activations, gradients, and any other process-resident tensors), mbaselinem_{\mathrm{baseline}} is the value of mtm_{t} immediately before the procedure begins (subtracted so the metric isolates the procedure’s contribution from any pre-existing footprint such as the runtime and imported libraries), and division by 102431024^{3} converts bytes to gigabytes. Lower memory indicates better efficiency; higher memory indicates worse efficiency.

Compute Utilisation. Compute utilisation is the time-averaged percentage of accelerator compute resources used by the process during unlearning on the active accelerator (see Table 2) [14]:

Util≔1N​∑i=1Nui∈[0,100],\mathrm{Util}\coloneqq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}u_{i}\in[0,100], (14)

where ui∈[0,100]u_{i}\in[0,100] is the percentage of accelerator compute used by the process at the ii-th measurement, and N=f​TN=fT is the number of measurements collected at sampling rate ff Hz over duration TT seconds defined in Eq. 12 (a typical default is f=10f=10 Hz). Lower utilisation indicates better efficiency; higher utilisation indicates worse efficiency.

Appendix 0.C Pins face additional results

Appendix 0.D Ethical considerations

SUPREME is an evaluation framework for machine unlearning methods. It is method-agnostic and introduces no new unlearning method; it standardises how existing methods are compared. The demonstration uses Pins Face Recognition, a publicly available academic benchmark of celebrity images. Identity is used as the classification target only to test whether identity-level information can be removed from a trained model. We do not propose or endorse face recognition as a deployed application. The full-class scenario uses five public-figure identities from the dataset to illustrate targeted forgetting. SUPREME is a technical evaluation framework. Low forget-set accuracy or small parametric distance under our metrics does not constitute legal verification of data erasure under any specific regulation.
